 Duncan Ferguson was appointed Glentoran manager last month
 Credit : PA/Adam Harwood
 Dominic King
 Merseyside Football Reporter, 
 in Belfast
 Published 
 07 November 2026 6:00am GMT
 This is a first. It was once easier to get an audience at Buckingham Palace than securing time with Duncan Ferguson, but things have changed so much he is now momentarily halting our conversation to get his phone so he can provide specifics about the tale he is telling.
 “Hold on a wee minute,” says Ferguson, proud as punch to be the new manager of Glentoran, as he rushes into his office before returning to our pew in the adjacent captain’s lounge. You’ll appreciate why accuracy is essential as he is about to relay a message Sir Alex Ferguson recently sent to him.
 “I couldnae believe his dad played here,” he says, those piercing blue eyes of his widening in amazement.
 Glentoran are a club who drip with stories. They turned down George Best, who used to be brought here by his grandfather, when he was 13 as he was “too small” and went head-to-head with Juventus, Benfica, CSKA Sofia and Marseille in the European Cup, nights that are still fondly recalled.
 Glentoran famously turned down George Best (left) for being too small
 Credit : Getty Images/A Jones
 Manchester United’s greatest manager even brought a team here, for a friendly, in 2007, but his unrelated namesake, who was on the Old Trafford wanted list in the summer of 1996 when he was at his rampaging peak as a striker, was unaware why his progress will now be closely followed.
 “Aye,” Ferguson replies, studying the screen in front of him. “He says: ‘My dad played with the famous Irish players at Glentoran. He played with Peter Doherty, I think he won the cup one year.’ What is he? Nearly 86? And there is still remembering things like that. It just shows you, doesn’t it?”
 Alexander Ferguson did indeed play at “The Oval”, turning out at weekends when he wasn’t working at the Harland & Wolff shipyard, which is so close to Glentoran’s home, the iconic Samson and Goliath cranes – emblems for Belfast in the way the Liver Birds define Liverpool – are always in view.
 The Samson and Goliath cranes close to Glentoran’s ground are emblems of Belfast
 Credit : Alan Lewis
 “He also says: ‘Good luck and I wish you well, Big Man,’” Ferguson continues. “It’s Sir Alex, isn’t it? He’s a diamond. He’s just a good man, the same as Big Sam [Allardyce]. Lots of people have wished me good luck. They know what the stress of management is, don’t they?”
 They do, as does he. So why is he exposing himself to stress again? Ferguson, certainly, hasn’t taken charge of this historic club – Fifa officially stated in 2022 that their success in the 1914 Vienna Cup should make them recognised as the first winners of a European trophy – for financial reasons.
 Had he wanted, Ferguson could have continued sitting on the pundit’s sofa. His stock was high after a starring role during the World Cup when his input was so refreshing and endearing, ITV bumped him up to 10 appearances mid-tournament after originally only planning to use him eight times.
 Ferguson has received plenty of support following his latest managerial appointment
 Credit : Alan Lewis
 “My kids [Cameron, Evie and Ross] are my biggest critics. They always give me advice but they said I was all right, aye,” he says, smiling. “I had this message off them: ‘Dad, you were good.’ So I must have been doing something right!
 “When they asked me, I was nae too keen. I was bit worried because I still wanted to be a manager. I didn’t want anyone to think I wasn’t being serious. The more I thought about it, the more I knew it could be a positive. It’s the biggest show on earth and people seemed to like what I was saying.
 “Seriously, ITV were happy and they were talking to me about doing the Euros [in 2028] down the line. I think I made a good impression and I did enjoy it, the boys looked after me. I’d never been to New York before... my God what an incredible setting.
 “All you did was walk out the hotel, into one of those big American lifts like you see in the movies, up on to this terrace and there’s East River, Manhattan, the Brooklyn Bridge. I’m no kiddin’... I’ve never seen anything like it in my life, this incredible moving picture. It was like being in the movies.”
 "Wonderful player, fantastic player, could not run" 😅
Duncan Ferguson reminisces about his time coaching Colombia's James Rodríguez https://t.co/JsVRigfBnZ
— ITV Football (@itvfootball) July 7, 2026 
 So, perhaps, it is fitting this Everton giant has resumed his eclectic managerial career – which began with two brief stints at Goodison Park before spells at Forest Green and, most recently, Inverness – down the road from Holywood, where the world’s best golfer Rory McIlroy started to chase his grand slam dream.
 “It’s costing a lot to come here,” Ferguson, who is in digs in the city centre but has yet to explore because he has immersed himself in the role, explains. “I gave up a lot of the field. The last five, 10 years, everything has been steady, you know what I mean.
 “I’ve given up a lot to come here, but it’s a great chance. This is a great club and they’ve got great people. And when you are on the touchline? It’s like what Big Sam says: ‘A win’s a win.’ If you get three points, no matter what the level, on a Saturday, you feel great. If you lose, you feel like s---.
 “I love working. When you are out of football, a day becomes like a month, you know what I mean? You’re used to working every day. You’re sitting around at home, a week feels like a year, so you get itchy.”
 For all that Ferguson can hold a room with his stories, it frequently gets overlooked he is a football obsessive. He never cut any corners in his coaching career, starting off at Everton’s academy with the under-11s and putting his heart and soul into every role.
 It is there in front of us. Glentoran’s stadium is so close to Belfast City airport, the start of the runway is one kilometre as the crow flies from the pitch’s centre spot and Ferguson still turns his head in disbelief, during drills, as jets begin their descent with an almighty roar.
 Ferguson was appointed on October 19, out of the blue. The session he puts on is lively, heavily based on keeping possession and working in between the lines of midfield and defence. He was held in high regard by Carlo Ancelotti when they were together at Everton and Glentoran’s players, all of whom are professionals, are buying into the vision.
 Ferguson in discussion with Carlo Ancelotti during a trip to Manchester City in the 2019-20 campaign
 Credit : REX/Peter Powell
 When you see this, it makes you wonder why he has had to come to this most unlikely destination. Ferguson has his own thoughts: blaming himself, first and foremost, for accepting a job at Forest Green, in January 2023 when they were stranded in League One.
 He has another theory why it has been a struggle to get work – the reputation he received in a playing career in which he received nine red cards, eight of which came in the Premier League. It is a record he shares with Patrick Vieira and Richard Dunne.
 “I can’t get away from that,” he says. “That was just how I played football. But I’m not like that off the pitch, unless you are breaking into my house! Other than that, I’ve been all right! I have been in Liverpool since I was 22 and if you are a wrong ’un, you’ll get found out.
 “Maybe they can’t see past it. A couple of years ago, I should have had the Middlesbrough job. Michael Carrick had said he didn’t want it. I had smashed the interview; the two boys who interviewed me told they wanted to give it to me but they had to speak to [owner] Steve Gibson.
 “I thought I had a right chance of getting it. A couple of days drifted by, then the sporting director phones. ‘We’ve got bad news.’ Carrick had changed his mind and he went back to Gibson and said he wanted the job. So they went with him.”
 This is the softer, reflective side you wouldn’t necessarily see when he is on camera. It is easy to forget that he was once the most expensive player in the United Kingdom, the first £4m footballer when he moved from Dundee United to Glasgow Rangers in 1993.
 His spiritual home was Everton, for whom he played twice in between a spell at Newcastle, and scored 72 goals in 273 appearances, winning the FA Cup in 1995. When Ferguson was at his best, he was unstoppable – skilful, powerful, fearless. There were seven Scotland caps, but it wasn’t enough.
 Ferguson lifts the FA Cup after Everton’s 1-0 victory over Manchester United in the 1995 final
 Credit : Getty Images/Hulton Archive
 ‘Football was easy for me, but I took my eye off the ball’
 “Ah, I look back with regret,” he acknowledges. “The level I could have got to. When I was younger, I was up there. That is why I became the dearest player in Britain. I was at that level when I was 18, 19. Nae’body could stop me. Nae’body. Then I took my eye off the ball.
 “I thought I had made it before I made it, do you know what I mean? I had scored a whack of goals, I was the most expensive player in the country and I was destroying every defender I came up against. I destroyed Germany, who were the world champions at the time, for Scotland at Ibrox.
 “I was going to go to Bayern Munich at one point. Karl-Heinz Rummenigge had come to watch the game and they were very interested in signing me. They [all the big clubs] were all chasing me. Everton wanted to sign me when I was at Dundee United.
 “Howard Kendall, God bless his soul, rang Jim McLean up and Jim says to him: ‘I’m fining him more than I am paying him!’ I got fined all the time. But football was easy for me. Then I took my eye off the ball and I was too busy doing Matthew Street [a famed Liverpool city centre hotspot].
 “I started getting injured and I struggled for the rest of my career. Injections, operations. Any time I played, I was fine. If I had played more games, I’d have scored more goals. It was that simple.”
 Ferguson admits he is ‘addicted to coaching’
 Credit : PA/Adam Harwood
 Whatever regrets there are, however, will not be dwelled upon. This is a new adventure, which began with a 1-1 draw at Coleraine and continues away to Carrick Rangers on Saturday.
 It is potentially a stepping stone to something higher profile in years to come, and the only thing that is worrying him is what is happening to his beloved pigeons while he is away.
 “A bloody weasel was in the loft last week and took a head off one of them,” Ferguson, who will be 55 next month, groans. “It’s coming through the loft, into the roof and got to one of them. Honest to God. My lads saw it and scared it away, thankfully, otherwise it would have killed the lot of them.
 “I love the pigeons, I always have. I’ll never change. But I’ve just to get results now, haven’t I? When I walk out the room for the first time, everybody holds their breath and thinks I’m going to start throwing tables!
 “I’m cool with the players I’ve had, but I never raised my voice with them. No, don’t need. I don’t want to. I’m not that type of guy. I’m not like that! It a long road, but I have still got dreams. You have to dream. I’m addicted to coaching. I absolutely love it.”
